strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: few-shot/in-context adaptation to unseen partners in cooperative multi-agent settings, with potential relevance to human-AI collaboration.
Combines in-context learning/transformers with zero-shot coordination and evaluates on five Overcooked layouts against several baselines (BC, MEP, HSP, fine-tuning, meta-RL-inspired).
Includes a human-agent user study (36 participants) with qualitative feedback, which is valuable and relatively rare in this area.
Provides ablations on context length and trajectory shuffling, and reports hyperparameters, hardware, and training time, supporting some reproducibility.
Limitations are acknowledged, e.g., structured environment and lack of explicit mutual-adaptation modeling.
weaknesses: Critical methodological flaw: training query states s_h are sampled from the same context C used as input (Section 4.2, Appendix B.2). The transformer can therefore retrieve/copy the best-response action associated with s_h from the context rather than infer partner behavior. At test time the query state is new, creating a severe train/test mismatch that likely inflates the reported in-context adaptation gains.

Overclaim: the abstract/introduction state CooT learns 'without explicit supervision,' but training uses explicit cross-entropy supervision to best-response actions (Section 4.3). This should be described as 'without test-time parameter updates' or 'without fine-tuning.'

Human study is inconsistently reported and lacks statistical rigor. The main text says 36 participants each played eight rounds with one of four agents, but Table 3/Figure 2 imply each participant rated all four agents; Appendix D.1 says 8 episodes for each agent and 1600 timesteps total; Figure 9 instructions say 7 games with 7 different agents in each of 3 layouts. No significance tests, confidence intervals, or effect sizes are provided.

Missing important baselines, especially PECAN (the closest context-aware zero-shot human-AI coordination method), as well as COLE, Other-Play, off-belief learning, trajectory diversity, and ICL opponent-modeling methods. HSP-meta is a weak/strawman meta-RL baseline (reconstruction-only PEARL), so the claim that 'Meta-RL struggles' is not well supported.

The results do not support 'consistently outperforms': CooT is worse than HSP/MEP in Coord. Ring and worse than HSP in Asymm. Adv. by mean reward; in Bothway Coord. a simple BC baseline is very close. The advantage is concentrated in Multi-recipe and Counter Circ., and the 'overall' reward averages across layouts with very different reward scales.

Potential train/evaluation partner overlap or ambiguity: Appendix B.1 says the training pool includes 36 agents sourced from MEP and HSP, while Algorithm 2 selects evaluation partners from Π0. It is not clearly stated that the unseen evaluation partners are disjoint from those used to generate the training contexts.

Ablations are small-scale (mainly Coord. Ring), lack standard deviations for context length, and do not isolate the proposed mechanism—e.g., no ablation on whether query states are held out from context, on including rewards in context, or on alternative context representations.

Deployment details are contradictory: Section 4.4 says the context is initialized with T previously collected trajectories before deployment, while Appendix B.2 says it starts empty. This affects the zero-shot/few-shot interpretation.

Limited originality: the method is essentially supervised imitation of a best-response policy conditioned on partner interaction histories; the Hidden-Utility Markov Game formulation is adapted from prior work (HSP), and no theoretical analysis or guarantees are provided for why in-context learning should infer hidden utilities.
The human study lacks an explicit IRB/ethics approval statement, and the consent form mentions an irrelevant 'trace electron radiation' risk; minor, but the ethics reporting should be clarified.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and clearly motivated problem—adapting to unseen partners in cooperative MARL—and frames it usefully as partner-centric in-context coordination rather than task generalization. The HU-MG formulation and the best-response prediction objective are coherently described.

The inclusion of a human-agent study (36 participants, 8 rounds, blinded agent identities, ranking + qualitative feedback) goes beyond most coordination papers and provides some real-world evidence of the method's practical behavior.

The ablations (context length; step-wise vs chunk-wise shuffling) yield a concrete, transferable insight—that preserving long-range temporal structure in interaction histories is important for coordination, in contrast to short-horizon navigation settings.
Reproducibility is reasonably documented: training/evaluation scripts, hyperparameter tables, dataset sizes, hardware specifications, and training/inference time comparisons are provided.
The evaluation spans five Overcooked layouts and several baseline families (BC, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta), giving a reasonably broad empirical picture.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is thin. The core procedure—train a transformer to autoregressively predict a target action conditioned on a context of past (s,a,r) tuples—is essentially Decision-Pretrained Transformers / Algorithm Distillation applied to a two-agent coordination dataset. The 'HU-MG' framing is inherited from HSP (Yu et al., 2023), and the only substantive change is the dataset (behavior-preferring partners + best responses) and the prediction target (best-response action).

The central claim that CooT 'consistently outperforms baselines' is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1. In Coord. Ring, CooT (38.30/0.47) is below HSP (41.10/0.49) and HSP-ft (41.30/0.49); in Asymm. Adv., CooT (129.48/0.62) is below HSP (131.78/0.63) and HSP-ft (131.79/0.63). The abstract and introduction overstate the results.

The 'Overall' aggregation is dominated by the two high-magnitude, low-interaction layouts (Asymm. Adv. ~130, Bothway Coord. ~100), so the headline Overall gap (68.79 vs 55.72) largely reflects absolute reward scale rather than a uniform coordination advantage. This obscures the fact that CooT is not best in 2 of 5 layouts and is within one std of baselines in others.

Several baselines are weak or poorly constructed, undermining the comparison. HSP-meta is reported to perform *worse* than vanilla HSP (40.19 vs 55.72 Overall), and HSP-ft shows essentially no improvement over HSP (55.86 vs 55.72). A meta-RL/contextual baseline that is worse than its own base policy is not a convincing strong comparison, and the paper does not show that a properly tuned contextual/RL^2-style baseline could close the gap.

There is an unexplained inconsistency between the agent-partner evaluation and the human study. HSP is the strongest agent partner (55.72 Overall) but the *worst* human partner (40.5, below BC at 51.0 and MEP at 53.0). If the agent-benchmark ranking does not transfer to humans, this raises questions about what the agent evaluation measures and whether the human result reflects the intended mechanism rather than confounds (e.g., latency, style).

The human study is underpowered and limited: a single layout (Coord. Ring), 36 participants, and removal of the top/bottom 10% of scores further reduces effective N. No statistical significance tests are reported for the human results (e.g., CooT 63.5 ± 9.5 vs MEP 53.0 ± 5.1) or for the main benchmark comparisons.

Some claims are misleading. The abstract states CooT learns 'without explicit supervision,' but training explicitly minimizes a cross-entropy loss against best-response actions—i.e., it is supervised at training time (supervision-free only at deployment). Similarly, 'consistently ranked the most effective collaborator' is based on a small single-layout study.

Presentation quality is uneven: the main results table is dense and mixes layouts, the 'Overall' row is not clearly defined, and there are citation errors/inconsistencies (e.g., 'Sillito et al., 2023' for Lauffer et al.; 'Lu et al., 2022' for Lucas and Allen; duplicated/mislabeled references). These are minor individually but compound the difficulty of verifying the claims.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated framing of few-shot partner adaptation as an in-context learning problem, using a Coordination Transformer trained on trajectories from behavior-preferring agents and their best-response policies.

Empirical results are strong in coordination-heavy Overcooked layouts: CooT achieves 45.96 vs 29.35 for HSP in Coord. Ring Multi-recipe, 28.28 vs 21.37 in Counter Circuit, 101.93 vs 54.99 in Bothway Coordination, and 68.79 vs 55.72 overall in average reward.

Human-agent collaboration study is a significant strength: 36 participants, blind pairing, objective returns and subjective ratings both favor CooT (mean reward 63.5 vs 51.0 BC, 53.0 MEP, 40.5 HSP; best collaborative/adaptive ratings).

Ablations and analyses probe important properties: context length, trajectory shuffling, fine-tuning instability, rapid adaptation over episodes, and robustness to non-stationary partner swaps (Table 4 shows adaptation within 1-6 episodes).

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed dataset configuration (Table 5), hyperparameters (Table 6), hardware specifications (Table 7), inference time comparison (Table 8), algorithm pseudocode (Appendix E), and training/evaluation scripts in supplementary material.
Ethical treatment of the human study is appropriate: informed consent, compensation, anonymity of agents, and qualitative feedback are documented in Appendix D.
weaknesses: The central claim that CooT 'consistently outperforms baselines' is overstated. In Coord. Ring, CooT scores 38.30 vs HSP 41.10 and HSP-ft 41.30 (BR-prox 0.47 vs 0.49); in Asymm. Adv., CooT scores 129.48 vs HSP 131.78 and HSP-ft 131.79 (BR-prox 0.62 vs 0.63). The abstract and conclusion should be revised to reflect that gains are layout-dependent.

There is a significant train-test context distribution mismatch. Training contexts consist of rollouts between a behavior-preferring partner and its best-response policy, while deployment contexts contain CooT's own actions, which are initially not best responses. This shift is not analyzed or addressed, and it may limit early adaptation or generalization.

Missing direct comparison to PECAN (Lou et al., 2023), a context-aware zero-shot human-AI coordination method, and to other in-context RL methods adapted for coordination. The baselines are mostly population-based or generic meta-RL, which weakens the novelty claim relative to prior context-aware work.

Baseline tuning and implementation raise fairness concerns. HSP-meta uses a PEARL-inspired encoder with reconstruction loss, which may be a weak strawman; the claim that 'Meta-RL struggles' is overgeneralized from this one implementation. The fine-tuning baseline is also inconsistent: the main text refers to HSP-ft, while Appendix Table 11 describes MAPPO with varying learning rates.

The human study is limited to a single layout (Coord. Ring) and 36 participants, with top/bottom 10% outlier removal. CooT's adaptation is reported to require 1-6 episodes, but participants may interact with each agent for only a few episodes, and the study does not analyze context length or adaptation dynamics in the human setting.

No formal statistical significance tests are reported; several differences overlap within standard deviations (e.g., Coord. Ring, Asymm. Adv.), and some claimed advantages rely on small-scale ablations mostly in one layout.

The method relies on access to offline best-response policies and hidden-utility partner distributions. Evaluation partners are drawn from the same distribution, so true zero-shot coordination to arbitrary humans or out-of-distribution partners is not fully demonstrated despite the human study.

Ablations are narrow: context length and shuffling are tested mainly on Coord. Ring, and fine-tuning is tested on 9 partner seeds. Broader ablation across all layouts would strengthen the conclusions.

The training objective is supervised imitation of best-response actions, not direct optimization of coordination return. The paper's phrasing 'without explicit supervision' is misleading, as the model is explicitly supervised with best-response action labels during training.

strengths: The paper formulates ad-hoc teamwork as in-context best-response prediction under a Hidden-Utility Markov Game, which is a useful and reasonably original framing that connects ICL/DPT to partner adaptation under shared rewards.

The proposed CooT is simple and technically sound: train a transformer on context-query-best-response action tuples and adapt at test time by appending recent trajectories to the context without parameter updates.
Experiments are extensive: five Overcooked layouts, Google Research Football 3-vs-1 with keeper, and comparisons against BC, BC-RNN, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta, PACE, GAMMA, and PLASTIC.

The human study is a clear strength: 36 participants, IRB approval, double-blind agent presentation, quantitative rankings, and qualitative coding with manual verification. CooT is preferred as the best collaborator by 18/36 participants and achieves the highest human-partner return.

Ablations and analyses cover context length, temporal shuffling, dataset scale, partner-switch recovery, and evaluation-partner sensitivity, which support the claim that context-based adaptation is effective in few-shot settings.

Reproducibility details are reasonably thorough: algorithms, hyperparameters, dataset construction, compute resources, inference time, and baseline implementations are reported. Limitations, impact, and ethics are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: The central claim that CooT 'consistently outperforms' population-based methods is overstated. Table 1 shows CooT underperforming HSP on Coord. Ring (38.30 vs 41.10) and Asymm. Adv. (129.48 vs 134.01); gains are mainly overall and on coordination-heavy layouts.

Evaluation partners are drawn from the same HSP/MEP hidden-reward population used to generate training partners. The paper does not test truly out-of-distribution partner behaviors or hidden rewards, so the claimed generalization to 'unseen partners' is limited to the same behavioral distribution.

There is a context distribution shift between training and deployment: training contexts contain trajectories from best-response policies, while test-time contexts are generated by CooT's own possibly suboptimal actions. The paper argues this is mitigated by posterior sampling but does not empirically analyze the effect of exposure bias.

The overall return in Table 1 averages raw returns across layouts with very different scales (e.g., Asymm. Adv. ~130 vs Counter Circ. ~20), making the overall return dominated by one layout. BR-prox is more comparable, but the overall return is still highlighted.

Baseline tuning is uneven. HSP-meta receives a systematic hyperparameter search, but PACE and GAMMA/PLASTIC are adapted with less evidence of extensive tuning, which weakens the strength of those comparisons.
The human study ranks BC above HSP on Coord. Ring, opposite to the policy-partner results in Table 1. This discrepancy is not discussed, and the human study is limited to a single layout.
Presentation needs polish: inconsistent notation (CooT, COOT, CooT 4), an emoji in the abstract/title, repeated figure captions, and typos reduce professionalism and clarity.
No statistical significance tests are reported for main comparisons, and several gaps are within large standard deviations (e.g., Coord. Ring, GRF).
The method requires an expensive offline dataset of best-response trajectories (about 19 GPU-hours per seed/layout vs 5 hours for HSP), a practical trade-off that is only briefly discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: ad-hoc teamwork / few-shot adaptation to unseen partners, which is genuinely challenging and practically relevant for human-AI collaboration.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: two benchmarks (Overcooked across five layouts and GRF 3-vs-1 with Keeper), a broad set of baselines (BC, BC-RNN, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta, PACE, plus GAMMA and PLASTIC in the appendix), and an IRB-approved human study with 36 participants.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: the appendix provides dataset configuration (Table 10), hyperparameters (Table 12), hardware (Table 9), training/inference timing (Table 11), and evaluation pipeline details (BR-div, DPP partner selection).

Several useful supporting analyses are included: context-length ablation (Table 15), shuffling ablation (Table 16), data-scale ablations (Tables 18-19), partner-set sensitivity (Table 14), and partner-switch adaptation (Table 4).
Limitations and ethics are treated honestly: the conclusion notes the lack of communication and embodied settings, and the impact statement and consent forms are documented.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The method is a direct application of the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (Lee et al., 2023) to partner adaptation; the paper itself states 'our architecture builds on the Decision-Pretrained Transformer.' The contribution reduces to reframing 'task' as 'partner behavior' in the ICL conditioning, which is incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Misleading framing regarding rewards. The paper repeatedly claims CooT 'relies solely on sparse environmental rewards,' but CooT is trained by supervised imitation of best-response policies that were themselves produced by HSP training with dense reward shaping. The sparse-vs-dense comparison in Table 26 is therefore not apples-to-apples; CooT inherits the benefit of densely-rewarded expert demonstrations while the sparse population baselines do not.

Generalization claims rest on a weak foundation. Training data comes from the same HSP/MEP pool used to construct evaluation partners, so 'unseen' partners may be near-distribution. The sanity check is unconvincing: the JS divergence of 0.3314 between training and evaluation partners versus 0.2976 between a random policy and evaluation partners is only marginally higher, which does not establish meaningful distribution shift.

Baseline fairness is questionable. HSP-meta and PACE both underperform vanilla HSP, which the authors attribute to intrinsic failure modes; while a hyperparameter search for HSP-meta is reported (Table 8), the PACE adaptation and the fine-tuning baseline are less well justified. The HSP-ft result ('no clear upward trend,' Table 17) contradicts the general finding that online fine-tuning helps and likely reflects suboptimal learning-rate/adaptation design rather than a fundamental limitation of gradient-based adaptation.

Modest empirical gains. CooT loses to HSP on Coord. Ring (38.30 vs 41.10) and Asymm. Adv. (129.48 vs 134.01), and the few-shot adaptation curve in Figure 2 improves only from ~0.53 to ~0.58 BR-prox over 40 episodes. The 'rapid adaptation' claim is thus supported by a small effect.

Human-study reporting is incomplete. The Collab. and Adapt. rating scales are not defined, the number of raters/rounds per comparison is not fully specified for the ratings, and the qualitative analysis depends on an LLM coder (Gemini 2.5 Flash), which adds a subjective layer to the perceived-adaptivity evidence.

Presentation defects. Artifacts such as 'CooT 😜' and '(CooT 4)' appear in the abstract, method, and conclusion, and there are numerous typos and awkward phrasings, giving the impression of insufficient preparation.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: few-shot/ad-hoc coordination with unseen partners, where test-time adaptation without gradient updates is highly desirable.

The method is clearly formulated: reframe partner adaptation as an in-context best-response prediction problem, train a Decision-Pretrained-Transformer-style model on context-query-action tuples, and deploy with a FIFO cross-episode context.

The empirical evaluation is broad: five Overcooked layouts, Google Research Football 3-vs-1, a 36-participant human study, and many baselines (BC, BC-RNN, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta, PACE, GAMMA, PLASTIC).

Results show clear gains in several coordination-heavy settings, especially Coord. Ring Multi-recipe, Counter Circ., Bothway Coord., and GRF, with useful adaptation curves and a partner-switch analysis supporting few-shot/non-stationary adaptation.
The human study is a meaningful addition: IRB-reviewed, double-blind agent presentation, quantitative rankings, and LLM-assisted qualitative coding with manual verification.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: hyperparameters, dataset configuration, hardware, inference time, algorithmic pseudocode, qualitative-coding prompts, and the source of pretrained policy pools are reported in the appendix.
The paper includes useful ablations on context length, temporal shuffling, training-partner diversity, trajectory scale, and evaluation-partner sensitivity.
Limitations are discussed honestly, and the impact statement appropriately considers possible misuse of adaptive interactive agents.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated. The abstract says CooT 'consistently outperforms' population-based, fine-tuning, and meta-RL baselines, but Table 1 shows HSP > CooT on Coord. Ring and CooT is not uniformly best; the claim of being 'reliable for real-world human-AI collaboration' is too strong from a single-layout human study.

Novelty is incremental: the core mechanism is a DPT-style in-context sequence model adapted to partner-specific best-response prediction. Prior meta-RL/partner-modeling work (e.g., PEARL, PACE, LIAM, PECAN) already treats partner adaptation as a learning problem, so the conceptual advance is mostly empirical.

Evaluation partners are drawn from the same hidden-utility/event-based reward family and the same ZSC-Eval/MAPPO training pool as training partners. This tests within-distribution behavioral diversity rather than truly out-of-distribution unseen partner behaviors, weakening the 'generalize across diverse partner behaviors' claim.

There is an unaddressed train-test context mismatch: during training the context consists of best-response policy actions, while at deployment the context contains CooT's own actions. The effect of this distribution shift is not analyzed. Additionally, query-state sampling is inconsistently described: Algorithm 1 samples s_h ~ C, while the main text says query states are sampled independently from the context/uniformly from the offline dataset.

The reward-shaping framing is misleading. CooT is supervised on actions from best-response policies trained with dense reward shaping/hidden rewards, so the statement that it 'relies solely on sparse environmental rewards' ignores the expensive expert data generation and indirect access to shaped policies.

The hidden computational and data cost is substantial. Training 36 behavior-preferring and best-response policy pairs via MAPPO is not included in the reported 19 GPU-hours per layout, and the method assumes access to a large, diverse expert population, which limits practicality in new domains.

The human study lacks statistical rigor: no p-values or confidence intervals for ratings, no variance for best-agent counts, small N, and only one Overcooked layout. The 'double-blind' claim is also not fully substantiated.

Relevant few-shot/partner-modeling baselines such as LIAM and PECAN are discussed but not empirically compared. PACE is adapted into an HSP-meta variant rather than compared in its original form, and its hyperparameter tuning may not be fully optimized.

Theoretical justification borrows a regret bound from Lee et al. (2023) without proving that its assumptions hold in the multi-agent hidden-utility setting; the O(1/sqrt(K)) argument is heuristic rather than rigorously established.

Presentation issues remain: emojis in the title/abstract, 'CooT 4' corruption, inconsistent notation (π_i^br vs π_i^w), layout naming inconsistency ('Blocked Coord.' vs 'Counter Circ.'), and table captions that do not always match their contents.
